factor_scores.evidence_summary: Bridge2 surface: 3 audits (Cyfrin Mar 2023, Zellic Aug 2023, Zellic Nov 2023); last commit d7e66aa7 2023-11-28 'address audit comments'; no on-chain upgrades detected post-Nov 2023, so Bridge2 bytecode plausibly matches audited code. L1 surface: HyperCore binary has zero audits and is closed-source. At the protocol level the dominant TVL-bearing operational surface is categorically unaudited, constituting a material scope mismatch.

Bridge2: last full audit signed off November 2023 (Zellic follow-up patch review). As of 2026-05-07 that is approximately 891 days (29 months). Well above any reasonable recency threshold. L1: never audited - infinite recency gap. Bridge2 has no on-chain evidence of substantive code changes post-Nov 2023, but 891 days without re-audit at ~$3.58B Arbitrum bridge TVL (and ~$5.0B combined protocol TVL) is a meaningful gap.

Commit history shows explicit fix commits referencing Zellic Aug 2023 findings 3.1–3.6 and 4.3. Each finding maps to a specific commit (e5b7e068, 8c4a182a, 1c8d3333, 97225667, b198269c, 57df1c10). No evidence of unresolved medium+ findings. Resolution is consistent with audited code being the deployed state post-Nov 2023.

Bridge2: 2 distinct firms — Cyfrin (Mar 2023) and Zellic (Aug 2023 + Nov 2023 patch review). The Nov 2023 Zellic report is a patch-review, not an independent full-scope second audit; total independent firm count is 2. L1: 0 audits. For a $4.7B TVL protocol, 2 firms covering only the bridge surface with no L1 audit is materially below peer expectation.
Zellic is a Tier-1 / top-tier smart contract audit firm known for high-quality bridge security work. Cyfrin is a well-regarded boutique with a strong track record. Both are credible.

Cyfrin engagement: Mar 10–24, 2023; Bridge v1 predecessor deployed March 2023. Zellic Nov 2023 patch review followed by 'address audit comments' commit d7e66aa7 Nov 28, 2023 — suggesting same-week deploy. The final Bridge2 deployment for the Nov 2023 version appears within days of audit sign-off. No >60-day drift detected for Bridge2 EVM surface.

Self-hosted bug bounty at bugbounty@hyperfoundation.org. Critical up to 1M USDC, High up to 50k USDC, Medium up to 10k USDC. KYC/KYB required. NOT on Immunefi or Cantina — no third-party verification of payout history or scope enforcement.

No evidence in public post-mortems that a disclosed vulnerability was reported and not actioned before an exploit. The bridge outage (Oct 2024) was an RPC edge case, not a prior-disclosed bug. JELLY incident was a market manipulation exploit, not a code vulnerability.

No formal verification (Certora, Halmos, Kani, or equivalent) has been applied to Bridge2 or any Hyperliquid contract. No FV report referenced in the audit docs or GitHub. Web search found no Certora/Halmos/Mythril application to Hyperliquid.

No published Slither/Mythril/Semgrep analysis of Bridge2 deployed bytecode found in public sources. Manual audits (Zellic, Cyfrin) covered the same surface; automated tool output not separately disclosed. Bridge2 source is small (~400 LOC). Tool run needed for definitive score.
Bridge2.sol source analysis confirms NO selfdestruct opcode anywhere in Bridge2.sol or Signature.sol. Contract is designed for persistence.
Bridge2.sol source analysis confirms NO delegatecall usage anywhere in the contract. Direct function calls only.
Bridge2 uses SafeERC20 for USDC transfers (whitelisted target by address), not arbitrary call with user-controlled target. No arbitrary .call(target, data) pattern found.

Bridge2 imports OZ ReentrancyGuard. The nonReentrant modifier is applied to batchedRequestWithdrawals(), batchedFinalizeWithdrawals(), and batchedDepositWithPermit() — all three externally-calling state-mutating functions.
Bridge2 integrates only native USDC (ERC-20 only, no callbacks). No ERC-777, ERC-1155, or ERC-721 token standards used. The nonReentrant guard also covers the ERC-20 transfer path.

No published Slither output available. Bridge2 is primarily a signature-validation and fund-transfer contract with minimal arithmetic. Validator power calculations use proportional arithmetic, but no divide-before-multiply was identified during manual source review. Not confirmed without tool run.
Bridge2 handles a single token (USDC, 6 decimals) with no cross-token arithmetic. No mixed-decimals risk.

Bridge2 uses Solidity 0.8.x with built-in overflow/underflow protection. uint64 power/threshold arithmetic is the main arithmetic surface; no signed-unsigned conversion paths found in manual review. Symbolic exec needed for full confirmation.

Signature.sol recoverSigner() function explicitly calls ecrecover(digest, sig.v, bytes32(sig.r), bytes32(sig.s)) and then checks require(signerRecovered != address(0), 'Invalid signature, recovered the zero address'). Zero-address guard is present.

Bridge2/Signature.sol uses EIP-712 style message construction. Commit 97225667 'Fix 3.4 Signatures may be reused across different contracts' directly addresses cross-contract replay prevention, implying some form of contract-binding in the domain separator. Full domain separator construction (including chainId presence) not fully extractable from available sources without direct code diff of that commit.

Bridge2 does NOT use UUPS proxy pattern. The AdminUpgradeabilityProxy pattern is used — upgrade authorization is via the proxy admin (Foundation multisig), not UUPS internal gate. Factor is N/A for the transparent/admin proxy pattern in use.

Bridge2.sol uses a constructor for all initialization. There is NO initialize() function in Bridge2.sol or Signature.sol. The AdminUpgradeabilityProxy pattern wraps Bridge2, but the implementation itself uses a constructor-only initialization path. Not applicable.

Bridge2.sol uses a constructor but does NOT call _disableInitializers(). Since Bridge2 does not use an initializer pattern (uses a real constructor), the OZ guidance is not structurally required — the constructor IS the initialization. However, defense-in-depth practice would still apply _disableInitializers() to prevent any future confusion. Slightly below best practice for a proxy-wrapped contract.

Bridge2.sol is approximately 400–500 LOC. Signature.sol is ~50 LOC. Total codebase under 600 LOC with 3 audit engagements. LOC/audit-day ratio is well within credible audit coverage range for the Bridge2 EVM surface. L1 binary complexity is unknowable but Bridge2 is the assessed surface.

Bridge2 proxy admin is a Hyper Foundation multisig (undisclosed address, threshold unknown). L1 critical operations require 2/3 stake-weighted cold-validator quorum. Operational parameters controlled by Hyperliquid Labs via closed-source L1 binary. Classification: multisig without timelock on upgrades. Admin type is multisig but transparency is low.

Bridge2 hot-validator quorum: effectively 3-of-4 for withdrawals (2/3 stake-weighted). Lockers: 2-of-5 to pause. Cold validator set: 4 nodes, 2/3 required for emergency ops. Proxy admin upgrade multisig: threshold NOT publicly disclosed (safe_api_gap: true). L1 validator governance: top-24 by stake, 2/3 BFT quorum.
Bridge2 proxy admin is Hyper Foundation multisig, not a single EOA. L1 critical ops require 2/3 cold-validator quorum. No evidence of solo EOA holding admin rights. Not a single-EOA pattern.

Bridge2 is verified/exact-match and no proxy upgrades were identified in the reviewed public contract state, so the proxy-admin-threshold wording is removed. Bridge actions require validator-signature consensus, but Hyper Foundation stake concentration and bridge-class TVL centralization concerns remain below green peer norm. Score remains yellow.
factor_scores.notes: factual-correction #58; accepted after second review where required

factor_scores.evidence_summary: Initial 4-validator set was entirely Hyperliquid Labs team members — maximum co-hosting. Post-expansion, independent analysis (Jan 2025) suggests 7 of 11 independent validators have questionable independence. No public key-custody attestations from validators. Closed-source node software prevents external validation.

Hyperliquid's hot validator set signs withdrawals with online keys by design - hot-wallet usage is structural, not incidental. Cold-wallet set holds administrative override keys. The hot/cold split is the architecture; persistent hot-key signing creates ongoing compromise risk at ~$3.58B Arbitrum Bridge2 TVL (2026-05-07).

Validator set expanded from 4 (Hyperliquid Labs) to 16 (early 2025) to 21+ (April 2025). Post-JELLY, on-chain delisting validation implemented. Positive direction (progressive decentralization) but Foundation still holds supermajority stake. Rotation from all-Labs to partial-external over ~18 months for $4.73B system.

No timelock is disclosed for Bridge2 proxy-admin upgrades. The withdrawal dispute period is a challenge window for withdrawals, not an upgrade timelock. The public analysis cited describes the upgrade path as immediately executable after the required signatures.

No action in Bridge2 routes through a governance timelock: (a) Proxy admin upgrade — no timelock; (b) invalidateWithdrawals() — cold-validator quorum, no time delay; (c) changeDisputePeriodSeconds() — cold-validator quorum, no timelock; (d) changeLockerThreshold() — cold-validator quorum, no timelock. 200-second dispute queue on withdrawals is operational safety, not governance timelock.

Lockers role (2-of-5) is distinct from proxy admin upgrader role. Lockers can pause bridge but cannot upgrade implementation. Cold validators execute emergencyUnlock but cannot upgrade Bridge2. Structural role separation confirmed within Bridge2 contract.

Bridge2 roles structurally separated: proxy admin (upgrades) vs lockers (pause) vs finalizers (withdrawal execution) vs cold validators (parameter changes). Fee collection and oracle configuration are L1-side, controlled by Hyperliquid Labs via closed-source binary — not visible or separable at EVM layer.

HYPE voting/validator stake is not flash-loanable current wallet balance. Delegation has a 1-day lockup, withdrawals from staking to spot have a 7-day queue, and validator stake is epoch-static for consensus. The rapid JELLY validator vote is a governance-process concern, not evidence of flash-loanable voting weight under RD-F-036.
factor_scores.notes: factual-correction #58; accepted after second review where required

factor_scores.evidence_summary: Not flash-loan-exploitable (HYPE staking lockup prevents instantaneous quorum acquisition). However, Hyper Foundation holds >50% of staked HYPE through its 5 validators — the Foundation already has supermajority quorum unilaterally without any market action. Concentration risk rather than flash-loan risk.

Documented governance votes (December 2025 HYPE burn) used 3–7 day windows. JELLY incident: emergency delisting executed in ~2 minutes with zero enforced delay. No formal minimum execution delay for governance proposals. Emergency actions can execute without delay.

No on-chain governor or proposal execution contract exists. HIPs are stake-weighted validator declarations, not smart-contract proposal payloads with delegatecall execution. Bridge2 contains no proposal execution path. Not applicable for this architecture.

Lockers set (2-of-5) can pause bridge functioning as circuit-breaker. Cold validator quorum provides second tier for parameter changes. However, neither Lockers nor cold validators can veto a Foundation proxy admin upgrade or a governance HIP. No veto mechanism against upgrade decisions.

Bridge2 has invalidateWithdrawals() (cold validator 2/3 quorum — can cancel pending withdrawals of any user) and emergencyUnlock() (cold validator 2/3 quorum). No timelock on either. Cold validator set is primarily Hyperliquid Labs-controlled. Quorum requirement provides meaningful resistance vs. single-key rescue. Yellow not red because the 2/3 cold-validator quorum is a real barrier.

No mint function exists on Bridge2 or any identified Hyperliquid EVM contract. Bridge2 handles USDC transfers only. HYPE token has a fixed genesis allocation with no admin-callable ongoing mint mechanism in publicly available code.
Bridge2 deployed mid-2023; proxy admin set to Foundation multisig from deployment per multiple independent analyses. No evidence of deployer EOA remaining as admin beyond 7 days post-deploy.

The public Bridge2 contract record identifies the bridge contract, but the effective proxy-admin address is not disclosed in the public material reviewed. Its transaction counterparties therefore cannot be assessed.

Bridge2 constructor args (initial hot/cold validator addresses, USDC address, dispute period, block duration, locker threshold) reviewed by Cyfrin March 2023 audit and Zellic August 2023 audit. No governance proposal voted on constructor args (pre-DAO era deployment). No evidence of silent arg deviation.

Bridge2.sol source verified on Arbiscan (verification submitted December 5, 2023 per search evidence). GitHub source publicly available at hyperliquid-dex/contracts. ABI is public. Audited by Zellic Aug 2023 and Nov 2023.

Hyper Foundation operates 5 validators with >50% of staked HYPE. Team HYPE allocation is ~23.8% of total supply (vesting). Foundation validators hold supermajority governance power. December 2025 USDH vote removed team HYPE from weighting — acknowledging concentration concern. Qualitative Gini assessment: extreme concentration at the validator level.

Hyperliquid documents a validator-computed weighted median of eight CEX and Hyperliquid spot mid prices. This is an in-house oracle built from spot venues rather than a documented Chainlink, Pyth, or RedStone feed, so it does not meet v1.7's established-aggregator standard.

The documented validator median is used for funding and contributes to the mark price used for margining, liquidations, and TP/SL triggers. The documentation does not identify a secondary or fallback oracle for those markets; all described sources are inputs to the same validator-median path.

Public documentation identifies the CEX/Hyperliquid-spot oracle inputs and the Arbitrum Bridge2 path. These dependencies are materially documented, but the bridge and USDC settlement route remain non-redundant access and settlement dependencies; the full impact map is therefore not green under v1.7.

The oracle documentation describes weighted-median inputs but does not document an automatic secondary feed, a pause-on-source-failure policy, or a bounded last-known-price path. Multiple venue inputs provide partial resilience, but the fallback behavior itself is not fully specified.

A failure or manipulation of oracle input venues can affect funding and mark-price functions. The native bridge is separately validator-operated and uses a dispute period for withdrawals. The documented paths permit a bounded partial-impact analysis, but do not provide a complete published failure analysis for every venue and settlement dependency.
Not applicable: the documented oracle uses weighted median CEX and Hyperliquid spot prices, not a single DEX-pool spot oracle.

The oracle is a periodically published weighted median rather than a DEX TWAP. The public documentation does not expose a TWAP window because this factor's measurement does not apply to the documented architecture.
No DEX pool is documented as the oracle source, so a DEX-oracle pool-depth measurement cannot be made for this architecture.

The oracle is a weighted median across eight named spot venues and then across validator submissions; it is not a single-pool oracle. This provides the multi-venue medianization required by the factor.

No automatic oracle circuit breaker is documented. During the March 2025 JELLY event, validators reached consensus to delist and settle the market after the price move, which evidences manual intervention rather than a documented automatic deviation halt.

Neither the oracle documentation nor the documented response to the JELLY event identifies a programmatic maximum-deviation threshold. The documented intervention was validator consensus after the move, not an automatic thresholded control.

Validators publish oracle prices every three seconds, but the public oracle documentation does not specify a stale-submission rejection rule or a maximum accepted age. The cadence alone is not evidence of a staleness guard.
Not applicable: the documented HyperCore oracle is a validator-computed median of named spot venues, not a Chainlink feed consumer.
Not applicable: the assessed HyperCore product is a spot and perpetuals exchange; this pass found no lending-collateral LP-token pricing mechanism in the documented oracle path.

No separate third-party keeper or automation service is documented for the oracle or Bridge2 path. Oracle publication and bridge signing are validator functions, and bridge operations require a stake-weighted validator quorum.

At review on 2026-07-24, DefiLlama reports $6.102B TVL, up 2.8% over 30 days. It attributes $5.71B to Hyperliquid L1 and $392.05M to Arbitrum. This is a large, growing TVL base; the concentration signal is assessed separately in RD-F-064.

Not assessed. A protocol-wide, independently verifiable ranking of the top ten underlying wallet or depositor balances was not available from the public sources reviewed. Chain-level TVL is not a substitute for the required wallet-level concentration measure.
factor_scores.notes: A time-bounded wallet-balance enumeration and concentration calculation is required before assigning a directional score.

factor_scores.evidence_summary: Not assessed. Hyperliquid operates an order-book perpetuals venue, so liquidity depth requires a timestamped book-level calculation for each major market. The reviewed public documentation describes the venue and its liquidity risk but does not provide a reproducible 2%/5% depth snapshot for the review date.
factor_scores.notes: Obtain and preserve timestamped public order-book snapshots and calculate depth consistently before assigning a directional score.

factor_scores.evidence_summary: Not applicable. RD-F-066 measures lending-market utilization. Hyperliquid's documented product is a perpetuals and spot trading venue with vaults, not a supply-and-borrow lending market.

Yellow. Hyperliquid's public incident history records HLP losses from a March 12, 2025 liquidation-mechanics exploit (about $4M) and a March 26, 2025 JELLY manipulation event; the latter was contained and followed by risk-control changes. These adverse loss events warrant a yellow historical-loss assessment, while the documented containment and maintained platform solvency do not support a red call from this evidence alone.

Not applicable. RD-F-068 concerns collateralization in lending or CDP markets. Hyperliquid's documented liquidation model uses mark-price margining for perpetual positions rather than lending collateralization ratios.

Not applicable. RD-F-069 assesses an algorithmic or under-collateralized stablecoin issued by the assessed protocol. Hyperliquid's published contract specifications describe perpetual products rather than a protocol-issued stablecoin.

Gray. Hyperliquid's public documentation confirms that vault depositors share in profits and losses, but it does not publish the native vault share-initialization and accounting formula. The cToken-style empty-market/first-depositor risk therefore cannot be confirmed or ruled out from public evidence.

Gray. HIP-3 requires a perp-DEX deployer to maintain 500,000 staked HYPE, but that stake is not a seed deposit into a lending market. The protocol has no directly comparable cToken-market listing mechanism, so the factor cannot be scored directionally without grading by analogy.

Yellow. HIP-3 permits any deployer meeting the 500,000-HYPE stake requirement to deploy a perpetual DEX. Validators may slash a deployer through a stake-weighted vote for technical or protocol-correctness, uptime, or performance harms after deployment. This is permissionless listing with a substantial financial barrier and a limited post-deployment safeguard, not a pre-listing governance review of each market.
factor_scores.notes: Changed from red: the current HIP-3 documentation establishes a substantial staking threshold and validator slashing mechanism, so a red assessment is not supported by the current public evidence alone.

factor_scores.evidence_summary: Gray. RD-F-073 is a lending borrow-cap factor. Hyperliquid instead documents open-interest caps based on liquidity, basis, and leverage, including per-asset caps for HIP-3 markets. The public documentation does not provide sufficient market-by-market parameters to verify that these perps controls meet the lending-factor criterion.

Not applicable. RD-F-074 is specific to the OpenZeppelin ERC-4626 virtual-share offset. Hyperliquid documents native HyperCore vaults, not an ERC-4626 implementation, so that implementation-specific control does not apply.

Gray. Hyperliquid's public vault documentation says depositors share vault profits and losses, and its legacy vault-leader documentation specifies a 100-USDC vault-creation deposit. It does not publish the initialization or share-accounting formula for HLP or all native vaults, so the first-depositor/share-inflation guard cannot be verified.

The public Arbiscan record for the active Bridge2 contract establishes a June 2023 mainnet deployment. As of 2026-07-24, the protocol has been live for more than 1,100 days, exceeding the 12-month threshold.

The JELLY market-manipulation incident on 2025-03-26 transferred a large position to the HLP vault and prompted an emergency settlement. It is one material exploit-class incident; documented bridge and API outages are operational incidents rather than additional exploits.
The reviewed public incident record identifies one material exploit-class event, JELLY. The chronic threshold of three distinct incidents is not met.
The reviewed public record does not identify two exploit-class incidents sharing the JELLY attack's market-manipulation and oracle-liquidity root-cause cluster.

The last identified exploit-class incident was the JELLY manipulation on 2025-03-26. That is 485 days before the 2026-07-24 refresh date, exceeding the 365-day green threshold; the incident remains reflected independently in incident-history factors.

The JELLY response was rapid, with validators settling and delisting the pair after the attack. However, the public explanation does not provide a full independent code-level post-mortem or a complete recovery of the attacker's withdrawal, so the response is assessed as yellow.
Hyperliquid's public JELLY incident page documents the 2025-03-26 event and its response timeline, satisfying publication within 30 days of the most recent incident.

The published audits document Bridge2 engagements that predate JELLY. The reviewed public audit listing does not establish an independent re-audit or incident review of the JELLY-affected HyperCore logic after the March 2025 event.

The public DefiLlama API returned 90 daily TVL observations through 2026-07-24. Their population mean is approximately $5.61B and standard deviation approximately $441M, producing a trailing-90-day coefficient of variation of 0.0786, below the 0.15 green threshold.

The JELLY timeline records the attack beginning shortly after 12:50 UTC, validator action at about 15:00 UTC, and an official statement at 15:47 UTC. A roughly three-hour response to the first official statement is green under this factor.

The JELLY validator intervention falls outside the 12-month window ending 2026-07-24. The reported July 2025 event was an API and order-execution outage rather than a documented deliberate emergency-stop activation. No deliberate protocol pause activation was identified within the current trailing-12-month window.
No public report located of a protocol-wide pause exceeding seven consecutive days between 2025-07-24 and 2026-07-24. The reported July 2025 API and order-execution outage lasted minutes, not days.

The public record continues to identify Bridge2 at 0x2Df1c51E09aECF9cacB7bc98cB1742757f163dF7 as the active Arbitrum bridge. No protocol-announced retirement and redeployment to a new address set was identified in the trailing 12 months ending 2026-07-24.

Nexus Mutual publicly lists active Hyperliquid Core Single Protocol Cover. Its displayed capacity of about 6,100 ETH (about $10.2M at the refresh date) is materially below 20% of Hyperliquid's multi-billion-dollar TVL, so available third-party cover is present but limited.

October–December 2024: DPRK-attributed wallets (attributed by Taylor Monahan / MetaMask security and on-chain clustering consistent with Chainalysis attribution) deposited ETH ($476,489) and traded on Hyperliquid. Attribution meets the ≥2-sources threshold. The $476k ETH deposit meets the >$100k interaction threshold. Whether these wallets had a mixer withdrawal within 30 days pre-interaction is not confirmed via public data — requires Chainalysis private feed. At April 2026 assessment date no new confirmed DPRK interaction since the December 2024 response. Signal would have fired at the December 2024 event date if live. Current posture: cleared for the specific wallets, but baseline risk remains elevated given confirmed historical interaction.

The DPRK October–December 2024 trading activity (small-value ETH positions, total ~$476k) is semantically consistent with test-transaction reconnaissance patterns but these were actual trading positions, not direct partial-drain contract interactions with Bridge2. No documented small-value withdrawal probes from Bridge2 that fit the strict partial-drain definition. Signal does not fire under the strict threshold definition. Gray — not applicable under current evidence.

Bridge2 deployer address 0x1D4c01E15A637cB3cbaF86fFbb02E5A260D01fbc cannot be directly monitored via public Arbiscan (403 on direct fetch). L1 deployer has no EVM deployer EOA (L1 is a closed-source native binary). No unusual mempool pattern documented for the Bridge2 deployer. Structurally gray for the L1 surface; Bridge2 deployer activity not confirmed as anomalous.

DPRK-attributed wallets used standard gas prices during their October–December 2024 Hyperliquid trading activity. Activity was exploratory reconnaissance (position testing), not a MEV-race or priority-fee-escalating exploit attempt. No 5× EMA priority-fee spike from attacker wallets documented. Signal does not fire.

No contracts with Bridge2 bytecode similarity deployed by suspicious addresses identified in available public data. The JELLY attack (March 26, 2025) used a CEX market-price manipulation approach, not a contract-deployment exploit. No selector-pattern exploit contracts targeting Hyperliquid identified. Signal does not fire.

No known-exploit-replay call-pattern documented for Bridge2. The JELLY incident (March 2025) exploited liquidation mechanics via CEX market-price manipulation on Bybit, not a specific function-selector replay against Bridge2 or any EVM contract. Signal does not apply.

Not applicable to Hyperliquid's interaction model. Users deposit USDC to Bridge2 via USDC.permit — interaction is with verified USDC ERC20 (0xaf88d065e77c8cC2239327C5EDb3A432268e5831) and verified Bridge2 (0x2Df1c51E09aECF9cacB7bc98cB1742757f163dF7). No approval to unverified contract in the Bridge2 deposit flow. Structural non-applicability.

The JELLY incident (March 26, 2025) involved coordinated actions on Bybit CEX external to Hyperliquid smart contracts, not a sybil surge of identical-pattern transactions on Bridge2 or HyperCore EVM contracts. No sybil surge pattern documented for Bridge2 or L1 interactions. Signal does not fire.

DefiLlama reported $6.11B TVL on 2026-07-24 versus $5.93B on 2026-06-24 (+2.99%). The factor threshold is a >30% decline in a 60-minute window; the publicly available daily series shows no present breach. Hyperliquid remains observable through the public TVL feed, so the signal would not fire on the available current evidence.

Hyperliquid uses a fully custom internal L1 oracle: stake-weighted median of 8 CEX spot feeds (Binance weight-3, OKX weight-2, Bybit weight-2, Kraken weight-1, Kucoin weight-1, Gate IO weight-1, MEXC weight-1, Hyperliquid spot weight-1). Oracle is embedded in the closed-source L1 binary — no on-chain EVM oracle contract exists to monitor for deviation. Bridge2 does not use any oracle. The JELLY incident (March 2025) demonstrated real oracle-path vulnerability via CEX price manipulation (Bybit weight-2 manipulated), but the EVM-side oracle deviation signal infrastructure is structurally non-applicable to this L1-native oracle. Structural gray: signal cannot be wired to HyperCore oracle via EVM tooling.

Hyperliquid's primary risk surface (HyperCore) is a native L1 binary with no EVM contracts exposing lending markets, oracle contracts, or a governor contract that can be interacted with via EVM flash loans. Bridge2 has no oracle and no lending market. The JELLY attack used CEX market manipulation, not EVM flash loans. Structural non-applicability: flash loans cannot reach the HyperCore clearing engine or oracle module via Arbitrum. No flash-loan interaction with Bridge2 documented.

The official HIP documentation identifies Hyperliquid's improvement-proposal paths rather than a Governor or Snapshot proposal queue. Because the trigger requires trackable queued proposal states, the signal is structurally inapplicable to the documented governance interface.

The public bridge documentation describes validator-controlled bridge operations but does not publish an address list or upgrade-event feed for privileged administration. Without an independently verifiable current admin set, the live upgrade-monitoring trigger cannot be evaluated.

Bridge2 is designed to accept validator-set updates signed by the active set. The cited 2025 validator expansion is historical, not a current July 2026 signer-set event. No public current-state feed or pre-announcement record is available here to test the factor's live change-detection threshold, so a current alert posture cannot be determined from the prepared evidence.

Bridge2 is a USDC bridge, so the exposure leg is structurally material. A public spot snapshot on 2026-07-24 showed USDC at $0.999579, but this factor requires a >2% deviation on at least two venues sustained for 30 minutes. The prepared evidence has no multi-venue, time-series monitor, so it cannot establish the live trigger state.

Public sources identify hyperliquid.xyz as the official domain and document phishing/impersonation risk, but they do not provide a versioned bundle hash, DNS baseline, or current divergence measurement for the official frontend. Impersonators are assessed separately; the official-domain integrity trigger cannot be measured from the prepared public evidence.

Bridge2 uses validator-quorum signed attestations (>2/3 stake-weighted) for both deposits and withdrawals — this is a validator-threshold signature model, not a mint-without-proof architecture. The Bridge2.sol contract enforces hotValidatorSetHash validation before crediting withdrawals. No unverified mint pattern documented. Structural non-applicability: Bridge2 design does not expose the mint-without-proof attack surface.

The public bridge documentation describes validator signatures but does not expose privileged signer identities, geography, or signing telemetry. Those inputs are necessary to test the new-geography trigger, so public evidence cannot determine the current signal state.

The public GitHub organization exposes an SDK and a limited contract surface, but this assessment has no immutable reference set or event feed for force-push, branch, or release-anomaly detection. The current live trigger therefore cannot be measured from the available public snapshot.

Public reporting and the official support guide confirm impersonation risk, including fake ads and similar-looking domains. The factor's live trigger, however, is a sharp current increase in accounts or campaigns. The prepared evidence contains no dated baseline or public monitoring feed that can measure that change, so it cannot establish that the live threshold is met on 2026-07-24.

No on-chain Governor contract. No Snapshot space. HIPs (HIP-1, HIP-2, HIP-3) are the only documented governance proposals and were voted via stake-weighted validator declarations. No pending/executed governance proposal ratio baseline can be computed. Structural non-applicability: the signal requires a Governor contract or Snapshot space with trackable proposal states.

Public reporting identifies co-founder Jeff Yan and documents his prior professional history. Hyperliquid's contributor documentation also identifies iliensinc, who operates under a pseudonym. The reviewed public evidence establishes one core real-name identity, not the two real-name core identities required for green.

Jeff Yan has several independently published accountability trails, including a named professional profile and public conference participation. The public contributor material does not provide comparable independent professional trails for every core contributor, so the team-level result remains partial rather than green.

The reviewed public profiles describe Jeff Yan's background and Hyperliquid role, but do not establish verified successful prior protocol work for the full core team. No adverse affiliation is asserted; the absence of a verified positive history maps to yellow under the v1.7 definition.

The public Bridge2 materials identify the Hyperliquid bridge and its source code, but the reviewed public evidence does not establish at least six months of prior non-flagged developer activity for the contract creator. The identified-address history is therefore treated as unverified/fresh rather than normal-dev-history.

Public reporting on the separate HyperVault incident identifies it as a third-party project on Hyperliquid rather than an affiliation of the named Hyperliquid founder. The reviewed public profiles provide no verified rug or exit-scam affiliation for the identified Hyperliquid founder.

The public contracts repository exposes commit history, but it does not identify the author of the most recent admin-permissioned change or establish that author's repository tenure. The exact v1.7 measurement cannot be completed from the available public record.

The public bridge materials and explorer record establish the contract and deployer context, but do not provide a complete ENS or NameStone resolution result. The available public record therefore cannot prove either the presence or absence of an identity binding under the v1.7 test.

The public profile and conference material consistently associate Jeff Yan with the published Hyperliquid handle and role. This review found no public evidence associating that handle with a prior rug; no adverse reuse is asserted for the pseudonymous co-founder.

The public repository provides commit records, but this review did not establish a representative commit-hour distribution or independently verify a complete team geography for comparison. The timezone signal is therefore ambiguous under the v1.7 methodology.

Jeff Yan has appeared in a named public conference video and public audio interviews. The reviewed sources do not establish two recent on-camera appearances for the complete core team, while they do support a consistent public identity for the named founder; this maps to yellow.

The named founder has a deep public professional and conference trail, while the public contributor material offers substantially less independently verifiable information for the pseudonymous co-founder and other contributors. The resulting team-level OSINT depth is moderate.

Public reporting describes suspected DPRK-linked activity as external trading on Hyperliquid. It does not publish contributor payment addresses or a supported <=3-hop attribution from a contributor payment to a DPRK cluster, so the required trace cannot be assessed.

The public repository and bridge source expose code and commit history, but do not provide a complete public record linking every admin-rescue or ACL change to a discussion at least 24 hours before execution. The critical event-based measurement remains incomplete rather than inferring a favorable result from the absence of an identified event.

The public bridge and explorer records identify the relevant contract context, but this review did not obtain a public transaction-level funding trace or CTI result for the deployer during the 30-day pre-deployment window. The critical mixer-funding test is therefore not assessed as green.

Public reporting establishes that suspected DPRK-linked wallets used Hyperliquid as external traders, not a <=3-hop relationship to the bridge deployer. No public CTI-labelled transaction graph was available in this pass to test the critical deployer-path criterion.
Hyperliquid is not a fork of any upstream protocol. Bridge2 is original code; HyperCore L1 is a fully custom implementation. Profile §5 explicitly states 'Not forked / original.'
Not applicable — no upstream fork relationship exists. No upstream to publish patches.
Not applicable — no upstream fork relationship exists. No upstream disclosure could affect this protocol via fork lineage.
Not applicable — no upstream fork relationship. Divergence is 100% from any upstream because the protocol is an original implementation.
Not applicable — no upstream fork relationship. Fork depth = 0 (original implementation). HyperBFT is inspired by HotStuff but is not a code fork.
Not applicable — no upstream fork relationship. Audit coverage assessed independently under Cat 1.
Not applicable — no upstream fork relationship. Economic parameter divergence from an upstream audit is not measurable because there is no upstream.

Bridge2.sol imports OpenZeppelin contracts, but the public contracts repository does not publish a foundry.toml, package.json, or package-lock.json. The specific OpenZeppelin version and whether it was pinned cannot be determined from the public repository.

No security advisory flagging a malicious release in OpenZeppelin, SafeERC20, or other Bridge2 dependencies in the last 90 days (through 2026-04-28). No npm/crates.io malicious-release incident involving Bridge2's dependency set detected.

Bridge2 uses OpenZeppelin contracts but the exact OZ version cannot be determined (no manifest file). The use of 'draft-ERC20Permit' import suggests an OZ version from the 2021–2022 era (draft-ERC20Permit was later promoted to non-draft in OZ 4.9+). Earlier OZ versions may carry advisory-level issues. Without a confirmed version, a definitive assessment is not possible.

Bridge2 source is on GitHub (verified on Arbiscan) but no signed release tags exist for Bridge2.sol — repository uses master-branch model without tagged releases. Bytecode-to-commit matching not verifiable without signed release tags. L1 binary is closed-source — no reproducibility possible.

The public Bridge2 contract record and repository identify the bridge, but the public material reviewed does not establish a complete, independently verifiable count of proxy upgrades in the trailing 90 days. No upgrade-frequency count is asserted.

No timelock exists on Bridge2 upgrades (F032 red). Any upgrade executed in last 30 days would by definition be without a declared timelock path. Exact upgrade count in last 30 days not accessible (Arbiscan 403). L1 continuous hot-patch model implied by closed-source operations.

The prior red score overreached by treating closed-source L1 audit opacity and hypothetical proxy upgrades as post-audit bytecode drift. Official audit docs show Bridge2 audit coverage, and no specific material post-audit Bridge2 bytecode change or proxy upgrade was proven. Remaining audit-scope and closed-source L1 risks stay under the relevant audit-scope factors. Score narrowed to yellow.
factor_scores.notes: factual-correction #58; accepted after second review where required

factor_scores.evidence_summary: Zellic August 2023 findings (incorrect finalization checks, signature reuse, unchecked USDC transferFrom) were fixed and verified in Zellic November 2023 patch review. No known open fix-merged-but-not-deployed gap as of Nov 2023. Post-Nov 2023 visibility is absent (no audit).
No evidence of test-mode params in Bridge2. Cyfrin March 2023 audit and Zellic August 2023 audit both reviewed the contract; no test-mode findings reported in either audit summary.

Bridge2 uses AdminUpgradeabilityProxy (OZ pattern). No OZ upgrades plugin storage-layout check artifact publicly available. Foundation can upgrade implementation unilaterally — if a storage-layout change is introduced, state corruption risk exists. Structural to the upgrade model; not confirmed as exploited.

Bridge2 source uses a constructor-based pattern, but the public material reviewed does not establish every implementation that may be active through its proxy path. Reinitialization exposure for the effective implementation cannot be determined from that public record.
Bridge2 is a standard deployment (not CREATE2). No evidence of CREATE2 factory in Hyperliquid's EVM contracts.

Bridge2 source on GitHub and verified on Arbiscan — reproducible for EVM component in principle. However, proxy pattern means future implementations deployed by Foundation admin may not be publicly committed to repo first. L1 binary: not reproducible (closed-source).

Public material identifies the Bridge2 contract, but does not disclose a complete authoritative deployer-address inventory for the assessed surface. A trailing-30-day associated-deployment count therefore cannot be determined.
Bridge2 is the documented native Arbitrum-to-Hyperliquid bridge for USDC deposits and withdrawals, so the bridge-specific category applies.

The active validator set is determined transparently from the top twenty-four by stake. Public documentation establishes a validator set larger than the low-count failure case, but does not document the organisational and geographic independence required for green.

Deposits and withdrawals require signatures from more than two-thirds of staking power, and Bridge2 verifies cumulative signer power above that threshold. Custody independence is not publicly documented, so the result is not green.

Public validator documentation describes permissionless operation and stake selection, but does not provide a complete validator infrastructure, cloud-provider, region, or custody inventory. Co-hosting cannot be determined from public evidence in this pass.
The public Signature.sol implementation rejects a recovered zero address before accepting a signature, covering Bridge2's signature-verification path.

Bridge2 signs messages using a domain separator that includes the Arbitrum chain id. The documented bridge is specifically Arbitrum-to-Hyperliquid, but public source does not expose a generic source-chain-id field for every L1 message path; the evidence supports partial rather than full generic chain-binding assurance.

Bridge2 implements usedMessages and checks it before processing administrative messages; withdrawal requests are keyed by message and rejected when already requested, with separate finalization state. This is an equivalent one-use commitment scheme for the documented bridge paths.
Not applicable: Bridge2 verifies validator signatures and uses pending withdrawal/validator-set state; it does not use a Merkle-root inbox acceptance mechanism.

Bridge2 supports validator-set updates, but the public sources reviewed do not provide a dated, complete history of the current set's last rotation or a published rotation policy. Rotation recency cannot be determined from the available public evidence.

No public source reviewed identifies validator key custodians or establishes whether one custodian controls more than 30% of bridge validator keys. Custody concentration cannot be measured from public evidence.

The public bridge documentation identifies the Bridge2 contract and the validator-set model, but this pass does not have a reproducible public as-of bridge-balance snapshot paired with the active bridge-validator count. The TVL-per-validator ratio is therefore not determinable.

Public reporting describes suspected DPRK-linked wallets trading on Hyperliquid in late 2024. It does not establish this factor's required mixer-to-protocol path or a qualifying 30-day pre-interaction mixer withdrawal. Without transaction-level attribution for that specific path, the current factor cannot be measured from public reporting alone.

Hyperliquid's core contracts (HyperCore) are L1-native binary — no EVM contracts are exposed on Ethereum or Arbitrum for mempool probing via failing/low-gas transactions. Bridge2 on Arbitrum could theoretically be probed, but no failing-transaction pattern from DPRK-attributed wallets targeting Bridge2 specifically is documented in public sources. The DPRK trading activity was on-platform (L1 positions), not Bridge2 contract probes. Structural non-applicability to L1 surface; Bridge2 mempool probes not documented.

Hyperliquid's auditable surface (Bridge2.sol) uses OpenZeppelin AdminUpgradeabilityProxy — a well-maintained, actively monitored library. The L1 node software uses a closed-source binary; dependency audit is not possible. Python SDK (hyperliquid-python-sdk) is a user-facing tool, not a protocol security-critical dependency. No GitHub security advisories flagging malicious dependencies in hyperliquid-dex org repos identified as of assessment date. Signal does not fire.

The official support guide warns that similar-looking domains and impersonator accounts are a user risk, and public reporting documented fake Hyperliquid ads. The red condition requires evidence that a high-similarity impersonator domain was registered during the trailing 90 days. The prepared public sources do not establish that registration date, so a red finding would overstate the evidence.

No contracts matching a known Hyperliquid-exploit template (Bridge2 selector patterns) deployed by suspicious addresses identified in available public data. The JELLY incident (March 2025) was an economic/oracle manipulation attack via CEX pricing, not a contract-deployment exploit. No selector-pattern exploit contracts targeting Bridge2 identified. Signal does not fire.

The DPRK October-to-December 2024 activity aligns with the USPD 78-day reconnaissance baseline. Taylor Monahan documented DPRK activity beginning in October 2024, approximately 60–78 days before the December 23, 2024 public disclosure. Trading losses (~$700k) are consistent with reconnaissance-phase mechanics testing: position sizing, liquidation mechanics, withdrawal timing. The JELLY incident (March 26, 2025) is a separate event — attacker manipulated Bybit CEX pricing to drive HLP vault losses — providing the attacker community with a proof-of-concept for oracle manipulation via CEX price feeds. Reconnaissance time for similar L1 perps exchanges: 30–90 days per hack database cluster data. Yellow: the December 2024 DPRK reconnaissance timeline passed without a confirmed strike, but the protocol class reconnaissance baseline remains relevant, and the JELLY attack pathway is the most realistic near-term attack template.

The public repository security page is not a substitute for paste, credential, DLP, or infrastructure-log monitoring. No such public monitoring feed is included in the prepared evidence, so the credential-leak signal cannot be measured rather than assumed absent.

Hyperliquid's official Discord (discord.gg/hyperliquid) and X (@HyperliquidX) are the primary channels. The extensive fake-airdrop scam ecosystem operates largely through hijacked social accounts and Google Ads, not through infiltration of the official Discord or Telegram. No specific documentation of the official Discord being compromised by a scam-coordinator-watchlist-listed actor. Fake social activity operates externally from official channels. Signal does not fire under the strict threshold (official channel admin flagged on curator scam-coordinator watchlist).

Public documentation identifies Bridge2 as the current bridge, but it does not provide a complete protocol-announced roster of deprecated Hyperliquid contracts and their balances. The available public record is insufficient to determine whether every officially deprecated surface is below the $100K threshold.
factor_scores.notes: A complete public deprecated-contract roster and corresponding balances could not be established from the reviewed sources.

factor_scores.evidence_summary: No formally deprecated contracts identified. Earlier bridge iteration superseded by Bridge2 with no evidence of retained admin control or material value held in deprecated surface. Not applicable.
No deprecated router identified for Bridge2. The bridge is a single-contract USDC transfer model — no router approval pattern exists. Not applicable.

Bridge2.sol declares pragma solidity ^0.8.9. The ^ range pragma means the actual compiled version was selected by the build toolchain and could be anywhere from 0.8.9 to the latest 0.8.x at time of compilation. Arbiscan returned 403 during assessment — exact compiled version unconfirmed. Solidity 0.8.28–0.8.33 contains a high-severity TransientStorageClearingHelperCollision bug; Bridge2 does NOT use transient storage (no TSTORE/TLOAD), so this known bug is not applicable. Most critical known bugs in 0.8.9+ range are not applicable to Bridge2's simple storage pattern, but the exact version is not confirmed.
Not applicable. Bridge2 is an original design, not a copy of any audited protocol. No bytecode similarity analysis against upstream is relevant. Profile §5 confirms original implementation.

No AI-tool co-authorship (Co-authored-by: github-actions[bot] or similar) found in the Bridge2 commit history. All 24 commits appear to be from human authors addressing specific finding numbers or making functional changes. The repo is small and commit messages are highly specific.

No public disclosure (blog, tweet, docs, forum) from Hyperliquid Labs or Hyper Foundation mentioning AI-generated Solidity in Bridge2 or any security-critical code path. Web search found no such disclosure.
Pragma ^0.8.9 is not an EOL version — 0.8.x is the current maintained series and 0.8.9+ is within active maintenance scope. No EOL version usage in Bridge2 or its OZ dependencies.
Hyperliquid publishes a bug bounty with a dedicated submission email and stated critical, high, and medium payout tiers. This is a public security-disclosure channel.
The public bug-bounty page provides a disclosure channel and payout information, but does not publish an acknowledgment-time service-level agreement. The absence of a public SLA is yellow.

The reviewed JELLY incident material describes a market-manipulation attack and response, not a vulnerability previously disclosed to Hyperliquid and ignored before exploitation. No public evidence of that pattern was identified.

A refresh-date search of the public GitHub Advisory Database and CVE records found no advisory explicitly naming Hyperliquid or the hyperliquid-dex codebase. No CVE or GHSA identifier was identified for this protocol.
Not applicable: the documented Bridge2 implementation is a custom stake-weighted validator-signature bridge, not a LayerZero OFT adapter or DVN configuration.

Hyperliquid documents an in-house validator oracle in HyperCore. Its public node repository distributes signed visor and node binaries rather than exposing the oracle implementation or an admin-replaceable oracle-address setter; the public materials provide no operational path to substitute the embedded oracle without a software upgrade and validator adoption.
factor_scores.notes: Critical v1.7 finding: the oracle binding is an opaque binary embedding with no publicly evidenced admin replacement path.

factor_scores.evidence_summary: Not applicable: HyperCore's documented assessed product is a spot and perpetuals exchange and its oracle consumes named venue prices; no lending acceptance of permissionlessly created DEX-pool spot prices is documented.

Bridge2 exposes locker-management and threshold-change logic, and its public documentation describes the validator-signature controls. The prepared evidence does not include a current locker set, current threshold, or event-monitoring baseline that would detect a reduction. The historical validator expansion is not evidence of a current threshold-reduction event.

The bug bounty program is self-hosted and describes scope as 'any bug that would cause an outage or logical error on nodes or API servers.' The scope does NOT explicitly enumerate Bridge2 or any Solidity contract addresses as in-scope. The L1 binary is mentioned via 'nodes' reference. $3.26B of USDC lives in Bridge2 but the bounty scope is framed around L1 node/API behavior, creating ambiguity over whether Bridge2 smart contract bugs are explicitly in scope. No Immunefi page with contract addresses to confirm.

The reviewed public reporting concerns external suspected DPRK-linked traders and does not identify a team contributor or external integrator persona with >=$1M attributed deposits used to build credibility ahead of a social-engineering attack. The cross-source attribution required for this manual factor is incomplete.

POSITIVE MITIGANT: Bridge2 Lockers (2-of-5) can pause the entire bridge. L1 validators can execute emergency actions in ~2 minutes (JELLY demonstrated). disputePeriodSeconds creates withdrawal challenge window. October 2024 bridge outage confirmed emergency lock functioned correctly (bridge locked, funds safe, unlocked post-diagnostic). No graduated per-window outflow rate-limiter - Lockers pause entirely. Significant positive mitigant for mass-drain scenarios at ~$3.58B Arbitrum Bridge2 TVL (2026-05-07).
